Government

In OG-Core, the government enters by levying taxes on households, providing transfers to households, levying taxes on firms, spending resources on public goods and infrastructure, and making rule-based adjustments to stabilize the economy in the long-run. It is this last activity that is the focus of this chapter.

Government Tax and Transfer Policy¶

Government levies taxes on households and firms, funds public pensions, and makes other transfers to households.

Taxes¶

Individual income taxes¶

Income taxes are modeled through the net tax liability function for each household taxj,s,ttax_{j,s,t}taxj,s,t​, which can be decomposed into the effective tax rates times total income and wealth, respectively, (61). In this chapter, we detail the household tax component of government activity taxj,s,ttax_{j,s,t}taxj,s,t​ in OG-Core, along with our method of incorporating detailed microsimulation data into a dynamic general equilibrium model.

(58)

Incorporating realistic tax and incentive detail into a general equilibrium model is notoriously difficult for two reasons. First, it is impossible in a dynamic general equilibrium model to capture all of the dimensions of heterogeneity on which the real-world tax rate depends. For example, a household’s tax liability in reality depends on filing status, number of dependents, many types of income, and some characteristics correlated with age. A good heterogeneous agent DGE model tries to capture the most important dimensions of heterogeneity, and necessarily neglects the other dimensions.

The second difficulty in modeling realistic tax and incentive detail is the need for good microeconomic data on the individuals who make up the economy from which to simulate behavioral responses and corresponding tax liabilities and tax rates.

OG-Core follows the method of DeBacker et al. (2019) of generating detailed tax data on effective tax rates and marginal tax rates for a sample of tax filers along with their respective income and demographic characteristics and then using that data to estimate parametric tax functions that can be incorporated into OG-Core.

Effective and Marginal Tax Rates¶

Before going into more detail regarding how we handle these two difficulties in OG-Core, we need to define some functions and make some notation. For notational simplicity, we will use the variable xxx to summarize labor income, and we will use the variable yyy to summarize capital income.

We can express household net tax liability taxj,s,ttax_{j,s,t}taxj,s,t​ from the household budget constraint (26) as an effective tax rate on income multiplied by total income plus an effective tax rate on wealth multiplied by wealth bj,s,tb_{j,s,t}bj,s,t​,

where the wealth tax function is described in Section Wealth taxes of this chapter. Rearranging the first term on the right-hand-side of (61) gives the definition of an effective tax rate on income (τs,tetr,xy\tau_{s,t}^{etr,xy}τs,tetr,xy​) as total tax liability, minus the wealth tax liability, divided by unadjusted gross income. And the definition of the effective tax rate on wealth (τtetr,w\tau_{t}^{etr,w}τtetr,w​) as total tax liability, minus the income tax liability, divided by wealth.

A marginal tax rate (τs,tmtr\tau_{s,t}^{mtr}τs,tmtr​) is defined as the change in total tax liability from a small change in either income or wealth. We allow these functions to vary by age sss and time ttt. In OG-Core, we differentiate between the marginal tax rate on labor income (τs,tmtrx\tau_{s,t}^{mtrx}τs,tmtrx​), the marginal tax rate on capital income (τs,tmtry\tau_{s,t}^{mtry}τs,tmtry​), and the marginal tax rate on wealth (τtmtrw\tau_{t}^{mtrw}τtmtrw​).

Note that a change in wealth bj,s,tb_{j,s,t}bj,s,t​ changes both income tax liability (through capital income) and wealth tax liability. However, it is both intuitively and computationally convenient to defined the marginal tax rate on capital income and the marginal tax rate on wealth to be separate, as we have done here.

Fitting Tax Functions¶

In looking at the 2D scatter plot on effective tax rates as a function of total income in Figure 2 and the 3D scatter plots of ETRETRETR, MTRxMTRxMTRx, and MTRyMTRyMTRy in Figure 3, it is clear that all of these rates exhibit negative exponential or logistic shape. This empirical regularity allows us to make an important and nonrestrictive assumption. We can fit parametric tax rate functions to these data that are constrained to be monotonically increasing in labor income and capital income. This assumption of monotonicity is computationally important as it preserves a convex budget set for each household, which is important for being able to solve many household lifetime problems over a large number of periods.

Default Tax Functional Form¶

For the default option, OG-Core follows the approach of DeBacker et al. (2019) in using the following functional form to estimate tax functions for each age s=E+1,E+2,...E+Ss=E+1, E+2, ... E+Ss=E+1,E+2,...E+S in each time period ttt. This option can be manually selected by setting the parameter tax_func_type="DEP". Alternative specifications are outlined in Section Alternative Functional Forms below. Equation (67) is written as a generic tax rate, but we use this same functional form for ETRETRETR’s, MTRxMTRxMTRx’s, and MTRyMTRyMTRy’s.

τ(x,y)=[τ(x)+shiftx]ϕ[τ(y)+shifty]1−ϕ+shiftwhereτ(x)≡(maxx−minx)(Ax2+BxAx2+Bx+1)+minxandτ(y)≡(maxy−miny)(Cy2+DyCy2+Dy+1)+minywhereA,B,C,D,maxx,maxy,shiftx,shifty>0andϕ∈[0,1]andmaxx>minxandmaxy>miny\begin{aligned} \tau(x,y) = &\Bigl[\tau(x) + shift_x\Bigr]^\phi\Bigl[\tau(y) + shift_y\Bigr]^{1-\phi} + shift \\ &\text{where}\quad \tau(x) \equiv (max_x - min_x)\left(\frac{Ax^2 + Bx}{Ax^2 + Bx + 1}\right) + min_x \\ &\quad\text{and}\quad \tau(y) \equiv (max_y - min_y)\left(\frac{Cy^2 + Dy}{Cy^2 + Dy + 1}\right) + min_y \\ &\text{where}\quad A,B,C,D,max_x,max_y,shift_x,shift_y > 0 \quad\text{and}\quad\phi\in[0,1] \\ &\quad\text{and}\quad max_x > min_x \quad\text{and}\quad max_y > min_y \end{aligned}τ(x,y)=​[τ(x)+shiftx​]ϕ[τ(y)+shifty​]1−ϕ+shiftwhereτ(x)≡(maxx​−minx​)(Ax2+Bx+1Ax2+Bx​)+minx​andτ(y)≡(maxy​−miny​)(Cy2+Dy+1Cy2+Dy​)+miny​whereA,B,C,D,maxx​,maxy​,shiftx​,shifty​>0andϕ∈[0,1]andmaxx​>minx​andmaxy​>miny​​
(67)

The parameters values will, in general, differ across the different functions (effective and marginal rate functions) and by age, sss, and tax year, ttt. We drop the subscripts for age and year from the above exposition for clarity.

By assuming each tax function takes the same form, we are breaking the analytical link between the the effective tax rate function and the marginal rate functions. In particular, one could assume an effective tax rate function and then use the analytical derivative of that to find the marginal tax rate function. However, we’ve found it useful to separately estimate the marginal and average rate functions. One reason is that we want the tax functions to be able to capture policy changes that have differential effects on marginal and average rates. For example, a change in the standard deduction for tax payers would have a direct effect on their average tax rates. But it will have secondary effect on marginal rates as well, as some filers will find themselves in different tax brackets after the policy change. These are smaller and second order effects. When tax functions are are fit to the new policy, in this case a lower standard deduction, we want them to be able to represent this differential impact on the marginal and average tax rates. The second reason is related to the first. As the additional flexibility allows us to model specific aspects of tax policy more closely, it also allows us to better fit the parameterized tax functions to the data.

The key building blocks of the functional form Equation (67) are the τ(x)\tau(x)τ(x) and τ(y)\tau(y)τ(y) univariate functions. The ratio of polynomials in the τ(x)\tau(x)τ(x) function Ax2+BxAx2+Bx+1\frac{Ax^2 + Bx}{Ax^2 + Bx + 1}Ax2+Bx+1Ax2+Bx​ with positive coefficients A,B>0A,B>0A,B>0 and positive support for labor income x>0x>0x>0 creates a negative-exponential-shaped function that is bounded between 0 and 1, and the curvature is governed by the ratio of quadratic polynomials. The multiplicative scalar term (maxx−minx)(max_x-min_x)(maxx​−minx​) on the ratio of polynomials and the addition of minxmin_xminx​ at the end of τ(x)\tau(x)τ(x) expands the range of the univariate negative-exponential-shaped function to τ(x)∈[minx,maxx]\tau(x)\in[min_x, max_x]τ(x)∈[minx​,maxx​]. The τ(y)\tau(y)τ(y) function is an analogous univariate negative-exponential-shaped function in capital income yyy, such that τ(y)∈[miny,maxy]\tau(y)\in[min_y,max_y]τ(y)∈[miny​,maxy​].

The respective shiftxshift_xshiftx​ and shiftyshift_yshifty​ parameters in Equation (67) are analogous to the additive constants in a Stone-Geary utility function. These constants ensure that the two sums τ(x)+shiftx\tau(x) + shift_xτ(x)+shiftx​ and τ(y)+shifty\tau(y) + shift_yτ(y)+shifty​ are both strictly positive. They allow for negative tax rates in the τ(⋅)\tau(\cdot)τ(⋅) functions despite the requirement that the arguments inside the brackets be strictly positive. The general shiftshiftshift parameter outside of the Cobb-Douglas brackets can then shift the tax rate function so that it can accommodate negative tax rates. The Cobb-Douglas share parameter ϕ∈[0,1]\phi\in[0,1]ϕ∈[0,1] controls the shape of the function between the two univariate functions τ(x)\tau(x)τ(x) and τ(y)\tau(y)τ(y).

This functional form for tax rates delivers flexible parametric functions that can fit the tax rate data shown in the scatterplot data in Figure 2 and Figure 3 as well as a wide variety of policy reforms. Further, these functional forms are monotonically increasing in both labor income xxx and capital income yyy. This characteristic of monotonicity in xxx and yyy is essential for guaranteeing convex budget sets and thus uniqueness of solutions to the household Euler equations. The assumption of monotonicity does not appear to be a strong one when viewing the the tax rate data shown in Figure 3. While it does limit the potential tax systems to which one could apply our methodology, tax policies that do not satisfy this assumption would result in non-convex budget sets and thus require non-standard DGE model solutions methods and would not guarantee a unique equilibrium. The 12 parameters of our tax rate functional form from (67) are summarized in Table 1.

Figure 3 shows the typical fit of an estimated tax function τs,t(x,y∣θ^s,t)\tau_{s,t}\bigl(x,y|\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{s,t}\bigr)τs,t​(x,y∣θ^s,t​) to the data for s=42s=42s=42 and year t=2017t=2017t=2017.

The underlying data can limit the number of tax functions that can be estimated. For example, we use the age of the primary filer from the PUF-CPS match to be equivalent to the age of the DGE model household. The DGE model we use allows for individuals up to age 100, however the data contain few primary filers with age above age 80. Because we cannot reliably estimate tax functions for s>80s>80s>80, we apply the tax function estimates for 80 year-olds to those with model ages 81 to 100. In the case certain ages below age 80 have too few observations to enable precise estimation of the model parameters, we use a linear interpolation method to find the values for those ages 21≤s<8021\leq s <8021≤s<80 that cannot be precisely estimated. [1]

In OG-Core, we estimate the 12-parameter functional form (67) using weighted nonlinear least squares to fit an effective tax rate function (τs,tetr)(\tau^{etr}_{s,t})(τs,tetr​), a marginal tax rate of labor income function (τs,tmtrx)(\tau^{mtrx}_{s,t})(τs,tmtrx​), and a marginal tax rate of capital income function (τs,tmtry)(\tau^{mtry}_{s,t})(τs,tmtry​) for each age E+1≤s≤E+SE+1\leq s\leq E+SE+1≤s≤E+S and each of the first 10 years from the current period. [2] That means we have to perform 2,400 estimations of 12 parameters each. Figure 3 shows the predicted surfaces for τs=42,t=2017etr\tau^{etr}_{s=42,t=2017}τs=42,t=2017etr​, τs=42,t=2017mtrx\tau^{mtrx}_{s=42,t=2017}τs=42,t=2017mtrx​, and τs=42,t=2017mtry\tau^{mtry}_{s=42,t=2017}τs=42,t=2017mtry​ along with the underlying scatter plot data from which those functions were estimated. Table 2 shows the estimated values of those functional forms.

Alternative Functional Forms¶

In addition to the default option using tax functions of the form developed by DeBacker et al. (2019), OG-Core also allows users to specify alternative tax functions. Four alternatives are offered:

  1. Functions as in DeBacker et al. (2019), but where τs,tetr\tau^{etr}_{s,t}τs,tetr​, τs,tmtrx\tau^{mtrx}_{s,t}τs,tmtrx​, and τs,tmtry\tau^{mtry}_{s,t}τs,tmtry​ are functions of total income (i.e., x+yx+yx+y) and not labor and capital income separately. Users can select this option by setting the parameter tax_func_type="DEP_totalinc".

  2. Functions of the Gouveia and Strauss form Gouveia & Strauss (1994):

    τ=ϕ0(1−(x+y)(ϕ1−1)((x+y)−ϕ1+ϕ2)(−1−ϕ1)/ϕ1) \tau = \phi_{0}(1 - (x+y)^{(\phi_{1}-1)}((x+y)^{-\phi_{1}} + \phi_{2})^{(-1 - \phi_{1})/\phi_{1}})τ=ϕ0​(1−(x+y)(ϕ1​−1)((x+y)−ϕ1​+ϕ2​)(−1−ϕ1​)/ϕ1​)
    (69)

    Users can select this option by setting the parameter tax_func_type="GS". The three parameters of this function (ϕ0,ϕ1,ϕ2\phi_{0}, \phi_{1}, \phi_{2}ϕ0​,ϕ1​,ϕ2​) are estimated using the weighted sum of squares estimated described in Equation (68).

  3. Tax functions from Heathcote et al. (2017):

    τ=1−ϕ0(x+y)1−phi1 \tau = 1 - \phi_{0}(x+y)^{1-phi_1}τ=1−ϕ0​(x+y)1−phi1​
    (70)

    Users can select this option by setting the parameter tax_func_type="HSV". The two parameters of this function (ϕ0,ϕ1\phi_{0}, \phi_{1}ϕ0​,ϕ1​) are estimated using ordinary least squares.

  4. Linear tax functions (i.e., τ=\tau =τ= a constant). Users can select this option by setting the parameter tax_func_type="linear". The constant rate is found by taking the weighted average of the appropriate tax rate (effective tax rate, marginal tax rate on labor income, marginal tax rate on labor income) for each age and year, where the values are weighted by sampling weights and income.

  5. Monotonically increasing smoothing spline tax_func_type="mono". This functional approach is based on Eilers & Marx (1996), Eilers (2003) and Eilers (2005), which is a least squares smoothing spline that penalizes nonmonotonicities. We used k-fold cross validation to show that the optimal smoothing parameter for this function on our tax data is λ=12\lambda=12λ=12, which is set as the default. These tax functions are fit to total income data (labor income plus capital income).

Among all of these tax functional forms, users can set the age_specific parameter to False if they wish to have one function for all ages sss. In addition, for the functions based on DeBacker et al. (2019) (tax_func_type="DEP" or tax_func_type="DEP_totinc"), one can set analytical_mtrs=True if they wish to have the τs,tmtrx\tau^{mtrx}_{s,t}τs,tmtrx​ and τs,tmtry\tau^{mtry}_{s,t}τs,tmtry​ derived from the τs,tetr\tau^{etr}_{s,t}τs,tetr​ functions. This provides theoretical consistency, but reduced fit of the functions (see DeBacker et al. (2019) for more details).

Income Tax Noncompliance¶

The parameters of the tax functions used in OG-Core are typically estimated using data that miss the effects of compliance (either because they use administrative data from tax returns or because of similar under-reporting in survey data Hurst et al. (2014)(see Hurst et al. (REStat, 2014))). OG-Core therefore offers the user two parameters that scale the marginal and effective tax rate functions in order to account for income tax noncompliance. These parameters are labor_income_tax_noncompliance_rate and capital_income_tax_noncompliance_rate and represent the rates of noncompliance on the respective sources of income. The implementation of these parameters is as follows. Let represent η\etaη the noncompliance rate (on labor and capital income) and let τ\tauτ represent the marginal tax rate (on labor or capital income) without accounting for noncompliance. Then, the marginal tax rate faced by a household, after accounting for compliance decisions, is τnc=(1−η)τ\tau^{nc} = (1 - \eta)\tauτnc=(1−η)τ.

When computing the role of compliance on the effective tax rate, we take a weighted average over the rates of noncompliance for labor and capital income. If we let XXX represent labor income, YYY capital income, and ηX\eta_XηX​ and ηY\eta_YηY​ represent the noncompliance rates on labor and capital income, respecitvely. Then the noncompliance rate applied to the effective tax rate is given by η=ηXX+ηYYX+Y\eta = \frac{\eta_X X + \eta_Y Y}{X + Y}η=X+YηX​X+ηY​Y​. If we use τ\tauτ to represent the effective tax rate, then the effective tax rate used in the households budget constraint and to determine tax liability is τnc=(1−η)τ\tau^{nc} = (1 - \eta)\tauτnc=(1−η)τ, where the η\etaη represents the average rate of noncompliance across income sources.

Factor Transforming Income Units¶

The tax functions τs,tetr\tau^{etr}_{s,t}τs,tetr​, τs,tmtrx\tau^{mtrx}_{s,t}τs,tmtrx​, and τs,tmtry\tau^{mtry}_{s,t}τs,tmtry​ are typcically estimated on data with income in current currency units. However, the consumption units of the OG-Core model are not in the same units as the real-world income data. For this reason, we have to transform the income by a factorfactorfactor so that it is in the same units as the income data on which the tax functions were estimated.

The tax rate functions are each functions of capital income and labor income τ(x,y)\tau(x,y)τ(x,y). In order to make the tax functions return accurate tax rates associated with the correct levels of income, we multiply the model income xmx^mxm and ymy^mym by a factorfactorfactor so that they are in the same units as the real-world U.S. income data τ(factor×xm,factor×ym)\tau(factor\times x^m, factor\times y^m)τ(factor×xm,factor×ym). We define the factorfactorfactor such that average steady-state household total income in the model times the factorfactorfactor equals the U.S. data average total income.

factor[∑s=E+1E+S∑j=1Jλjωˉs(wˉej,snˉj,s+rˉpbˉj,s)]=Avg. household income in data factor\Biggl[\sum_{s=E+1}^{E+S}\sum_{j=1}^J\lambda_j\bar{\omega}_s\left(\bar{w}e_{j,s}\bar{n}_{j,s} + \bar{r}_{p}\bar{b}_{j,s}\right)\Biggr] = \text{Avg. household income in data}factor[s=E+1∑E+S​j=1∑J​λj​ωˉs​(wˉej,s​nˉj,s​+rˉp​bˉj,s​)]=Avg. household income in data
(71)

We do not know the steady-state wage, interest rate, household labor supply, and savings ex ante. So the income factorfactorfactor is an endogenous variable in the steady-state equilibrium computational solution. We hold the factor constant throughout the nonsteady-state equilibrium solution.

Consumption taxes¶

Linear consumption taxes, τi,tc\tau^c_{i,t}τi,tc​ can vary over time and by consumption good.

Wealth taxes¶

Wealth taxes can be implemented through the taxj,s,tw(bj,s,t)tax^{w}_{j,s,t}(b_{j,s,t})taxj,s,tw​(bj,s,t​) function, shown in equations (61) through (66). This functional form allows for zero to flat to progressive wealth taxation and is given by the following,

taxj,s,tw=pw(hwbj,s,thwbj,s,t+mw)bj,s,t tax^{w}_{j,s,t} = p^w\left(\frac{h^{w}b_{j,s,t}}{h^{w}b_{j,s,t} + m^{w}}\right)b_{j,s,t}taxj,s,tw​=pw(hwbj,s,t​+mwhwbj,s,t​​)bj,s,t​
(72)

where pw≥0p^w\geq 0pw≥0 is a nonnegative scale parameter of the overall tax rate, hw>0h^w> 0hw>0 is a strictly positive scale coefficient parameter on the linear term inside of the parentheses, and mw≥0m^w\geq 0mw≥0 is a nonnegative constant additive coefficient in the denominator of the rate function in parentheses. This functional form allows us to represent a zero wealth tax rate (pw=0p^w=0pw=0), a flat wealth tax rate (pw>0p^w>0pw>0 and mw=0m_w= 0mw​=0), and a progressive wealth tax rate (pwp^wpw, hwh^whw, and mwm^wmw > 0).

The expression for the effective tax rate on wealth is the following.

τtetr,w=taxj,s,twbj,s,t=pw(hwbj,s,thwbj,s,t+mw)∀j,s,t \tau^{etr,w}_{t} = \frac{tax^{w}_{j,s,t}}{b_{j,s,t}} = p^w\left(\frac{h^{w}b_{j,s,t}}{h^{w}b_{j,s,t} + m^{w}}\right) \quad\forall j,s,tτtetr,w​=bj,s,t​taxj,s,tw​​=pw(hwbj,s,t​+mwhwbj,s,t​​)∀j,s,t
(73)

The analytical expression for the marginal tax rate on wealth defined in equation {eq}`` is the following.

τtmtrw=∂taxj,s,tw∂bj,s,t=τtetr,w[2−(hwbj,s,thwbj,s,t+mw)]∀j,s,t \tau^{mtrw}_{t} = \frac{\partial tax^{w}_{j,s,t}}{\partial b_{j,s,t}} = \tau^{etr,w}_t\left[2 - \left(\frac{h^w b_{j,s,t}}{h^w b_{j,s,t} + m^w}\right)\right] \quad\forall j,s,tτtmtrw​=∂bj,s,t​∂taxj,s,tw​​=τtetr,w​[2−(hwbj,s,t​+mwhwbj,s,t​​)]∀j,s,t
(74)

Corporate income taxes¶

Businesses face a linear tax rate τm,tcorp\tau^{corp}_{m,t}τm,tcorp​, which can vary by industry and over time. In the case of a single industry, OG-Core provides the parameters c_corp_share_of_assets to scale the tax rate applied to the representative firm so that it represents a weighted average between the rate on businesses entities taxes at the entity level (e.g., C corporations in the United States) and those with no entity level tax. The parameter adjustment_factor_for_cit_receipts is additionally provided to represent a wedge between marginal and average tax rates (which could otherwise be zero with a linear tax function).

Spending¶

Government spending is comprised of government provided pension benefits, lump sum transfers, universal basic income payments, infrastructure investment, spending on public goods, and interest payments on debt. Below, we describe the transfer spending amounts. Spending on infrastructure, public goods, and interest are described in Government Budget Constraint. Because government spending on lump-sum transfers to households TRtTR_tTRt​, public goods GtG_tGt​, and government infrastructure capital IgI_gIg​ are all functions of nominal GDP, we define GDP here,

Yt≡∑m=1Mpm,tYm,t∀t Y_t \equiv \sum_{m=1}^M p_{m,t} Y_{m,t} \quad\forall tYt​≡m=1∑M​pm,t​Ym,t​∀t
(75)

where GDP YtY_tYt​ is in terms of the numeraire good of industry-MMM output.[3]

Pensions¶

The OG-Core model allows for five different systems for public pensions:

  1. U.S.-style social security system

  2. Defined benefit system

  3. Notional defined contribution system

  4. Points system

  5. Hybrid defined benefit and notional defined contribution system

These can be selected with the pension_system parameter. Accepted values are US-Style Social Security, Defined Benefits, Notional Defined Contribution, Points System, Hybrid DB-NDC. We discuss each of these in turn below.

For all systems, RRR represents the age at which the individual becomes eligible to receive the government provided retirement benefit. The retirement age is a property of a birth cohort rather than of a calendar year: a household born in period t−st-st−s (of age sss in period ttt) faces the retirement age Rt−sR_{t-s}Rt−s​, and it faces the same Rt−sR_{t-s}Rt−s​ in every period of its life unless a reform moves its cohort to a new value. The base value is the parameter retirement_age. Changes are entered through pension_regimes, a list of reforms applied in order, each with a calendar year from which it applies, an optional max_age_at_start (the oldest age, in that calendar year, to which the reform applies; cohorts not yet born always qualify, and leaving it out applies the reform to everyone including current retirees), and the new parameter values. This is how a phased-in increase in the retirement age that exempts those near retirement is expressed. The model expands these inputs into an array over periods and ages, so the household problem, the aggregates, and the steady state (which uses the final period’s value) all read the same cohort-specific retirement age. The parameters of the defined benefit system (alpha_db, avg_earn_num_years, yr_contrib) and of the notional defined contribution system (tau_p, k_ret, indR) can be changed by cohort in the same way, so a reform of the benefit formula can also be phased in by birth cohort. With no regimes, the base alpha_db is a path by lifetime income group and the calendar year in which a benefit is paid, and the other parameters are single values. The replacement-rate adjustment replacement_rate_adjust is, by contrast, always indexed by the calendar year in which a benefit is paid.

US-style social security system¶

Under the U.S.-style social security system, households over age RRR received a pension amount that is a function of their earnings history. The earnings history includes the highest earning avg_earn_num_years prior to retirement (which OG-Core assumes happens at age RRR). This history determines the Average Indexed Monthly Earnings (AIME):

AIMEj,R,t+R=∑u=0AIMEperwt+uej,u,t+unj,u,t+u12∗AIMEperAIME_{j,R,t+R} = {\sum_{u=0}^{AIMEper} w_{t+u}e_{j,u,t+u}n_{j,u,t+u}}{ 12 * AIMEper}AIMEj,R,t+R​=u=0∑AIMEper​wt+u​ej,u,t+u​nj,u,t+u​12∗AIMEper
(76)

The AIME in turn, determines a household’s (PIA) based on three rates and brackets:

PIAbasej,R,t+R={PIArate1×AIMEj,R,t+R,for AIMEj,R,t+R≤AIMEbkt1PIArate1×AIMEbkt1+PIArate2×(AIMEj,R,t+R−AIMEbkt1),for AIMEbkt1<AIMEj,R,t+R≤AIMEbkt2PIArate1×AIMEbkt1+PIArate2×(AIMEbkt2−AIMEbkt1)+PIArate3×(AIMEj,R,t+R−AIMEbkt2),for AIMEbkt2<AIMEj,R,t+R PIAbase_{j,R,t+R} = \begin{cases} PIArate_1 \times AIME_{j,R,t+R}, \text{for } AIME_{j,R,t+R} \leq AIMEbkt_1 \\ PIArate_1 \times AIMEbkt_1 + PIArate_2 \times (AIME_{j,R,t+R} - AIMEbkt_1), \text{for } AIMEbkt_1 < AIME_{j,R,t+R} \leq AIMEbkt_2 \\ PIArate_1 \times AIMEbkt_1 + PIArate_2 \times (AIMEbkt_2 - AIMEbkt_1) + PIArate_3 \times (AIME_{j,R,t+R} - AIMEbkt_2), \text{for } AIMEbkt_2 < AIME_{j,R,t+R} \\ \end{cases}PIAbasej,R,t+R​=⎩⎨⎧​PIArate1​×AIMEj,R,t+R​,for AIMEj,R,t+R​≤AIMEbkt1​PIArate1​×AIMEbkt1​+PIArate2​×(AIMEj,R,t+R​−AIMEbkt1​),for AIMEbkt1​<AIMEj,R,t+R​≤AIMEbkt2​PIArate1​×AIMEbkt1​+PIArate2​×(AIMEbkt2​−AIMEbkt1​)+PIArate3​×(AIMEj,R,t+R​−AIMEbkt2​),for AIMEbkt2​<AIMEj,R,t+R​​
(77)

The PIA is then capped at a maximum, set by the parameter PIA_maxpayment, and, when the parameter PIA_minpayment is nonzero, floored at that minimum: PIAj,R,t+R=max⁡{min⁡{PIAbasej,R,t+R, PIA max payment amount}, PIA min payment amount}PIA_{j,R,t+R} = \max\{\min\{PIAbase_{j,R,t+R}, \text{ PIA max payment amount}\}, \text{ PIA min payment amount}\}PIAj,R,t+R​=max{min{PIAbasej,R,t+R​, PIA max payment amount}, PIA min payment amount}.

The replacement rate, θj\theta_jθj​ is then calculated as annual earnings, with an adjustment for the wage rate.:

θj,R,t+R=PIAj,R,t+R×12factor×wt+R \theta_{j,R,t+R} = \frac{PIA_{j,R,t+R} \times 12}{factor \times w_{t+R}}θj,R,t+R​=factor×wt+R​PIAj,R,t+R​×12​
(78)

Note that AIMEj,R,t+RAIME_{j,R,t+R}AIMEj,R,t+R​ is a function of each households’ earning history, but their choice of earning may depend on their retirement benefit. Solving this exactly would introduce and additional fixed point problem in both the steady state solution and in the time path solution. The latter would be extremely computationally taxing. Therefore, we make the simplification of determining the AIME for each type jjj using the steady state solution and earnings for type jjj in the steady state. This leads to some approximation error, but because θj\theta_jθj​ is adjusted by the current wage rate, this approximation error is minized.

The pension amount for households under the US-style social security system is then:

pensionj,s,t=θj×wt∀s≥Rt−s pension_{j,s,t} = \theta_j \times w_t \quad \forall s \geq R_{t-s}pensionj,s,t​=θj​×wt​∀s≥Rt−s​
(79)
Defined benefit system¶

The defined benefit system pension amount is given as:

pensionj,s,t=[∑u=R−nyR−1wt−s+uej,u,t−s+unj,u,t−s+uny]×Cy×αj,s,tDB∀s≥Rpension_{j,s,t} = \biggl[\frac{\sum_{u=R-ny}^{R-1}w_{t-s+u}e_{j,u,t-s+u}n_{j,u,t-s+u}}{ny}\biggr]\times Cy \times \alpha^{DB}_{j,s,t} \quad \forall s \geq Rpensionj,s,t​=[ny∑u=R−nyR−1​wt−s+u​ej,u,t−s+u​nj,u,t−s+u​​]×Cy×αj,s,tDB​∀s≥R
(80)

where the sum runs over the household’s own earnings history (the wage, effective labor units, and labor supply at each working age uuu were those of period t−s+ut-s+ut−s+u), and:

  • nynyny are the number of years over which average earnings are calculated (avg_earn_num_years)

  • CyCyCy are the number of years of contributions (yr_contrib). In our model, there is no exit from the labor force, so workers will contribute for RRR years, but CyCyCy could be some number less than RRR if there is a maximum number of years of contributions one can accrue under the DB system.

  • αj,s,tDB\alpha^{DB}_{j,s,t}αj,s,tDB​ is the replacement rate per year of contribution (alpha_db), which may vary across lifetime income groups.

  • RRR, nynyny, CyCyCy, and αDB\alpha^{DB}αDB are the values that apply to the household’s birth cohort t−st-st−s at the age and period in which the benefit is paid. With no pension_regimes, RRR, nynyny, and CyCyCy are the same for every cohort and αj,tDB\alpha^{DB}_{j,t}αj,tDB​ is a path by the calendar year of payment, so a change in it affects the benefits of current retirees as well as those of future retirees. A regime with a max_age_at_start instead changes the formula only for the cohorts it covers, so the benefits of those already retired are unchanged.

Given this pension system and the fact that there is only variation in labor supply along the intensive margin (so we don’t need to consider changes in CyCyCy), the partial derivatives from the household section are given by:

∂θj,u,t+u−s∂nj,s,t={0,if s<R−Cywtej,sαj,t+R−sDB×Cyny,if R−Cy<=s<R0,if s≥R \frac{\partial \theta_{j,u,t+u-s}}{\partial n_{j,s,t}} = \begin{cases} 0 , & \text{if}\ s < R - Cy \\ w_{t}e_{j,s}\alpha^{DB}_{j,t+R-s}\times \frac{Cy}{ny}, & \text{if}\ R - Cy <= s < R \\ 0, & \text{if}\ s \geq R \\ \end{cases}∂nj,s,t​∂θj,u,t+u−s​​=⎩⎨⎧​0,wt​ej,s​αj,t+R−sDB​×nyCy​,0,​if s<R−Cyif R−Cy<=s<Rif s≥R​
(81)
Notional defined contribution system¶

The pension amount under a notional defined contribution system is given as:

pensionj,s,t=[∑u=ER−1τu,t−s+upwt−s+uej,u,t−s+unj,u,t−s+u∏a=u+1R−1(1+gNDC,t−s+a)]δR,s,t∀s≥R pension_{j,s,t} = \biggl[\sum_{u=E}^{R-1}\tau^{p}_{u,t-s+u}w_{t-s+u}e_{j,u,t-s+u}n_{j,u,t-s+u}\prod_{a=u+1}^{R-1}(1 + g_{NDC,t-s+a})\biggr]\delta_{R,s,t} \quad \forall s \geq Rpensionj,s,t​=[u=E∑R−1​τu,t−s+up​wt−s+u​ej,u,t−s+u​nj,u,t−s+u​a=u+1∏R−1​(1+gNDC,t−s+a​)]δR,s,t​∀s≥R
(82)

where the sum runs over the household’s own contribution history, quantities are in real, non-stationarized units, and:

  • τu,t−s+up\tau^{p}_{u,t-s+u}τu,t−s+up​ is the notional contribution rate (tau_p) that the household’s cohort faced at working age uuu, in period t−s+ut-s+ut−s+u. It sets the share of labor income credited to the household’s notional account. It is not a tax: it is not deducted from household income or counted as government revenue. The only payroll tax households pay is tau_payroll, which applies to all labor income under every pension system

  • gNDC,tg_{NDC,t}gNDC,t​ is the rate credited to notional balances in period ttt. A contribution made at age uuu earns the rates credited in each period from the next one through the period before retirement. The credited rate is the growth realized from period t−1t-1t−1 to period ttt of the measure chosen with ndc_growth_rate. Because model aggregates are stationarized by egyte^{g_y t}egy​t and by population, the growth of an aggregate XXX is recovered from its stationarized value X^\hat{X}X^ as

    1+gX,t=X^tX^t−1egy(1+gn,t−1)1 + g_{X,t} = \frac{\hat{X}_{t}}{\hat{X}_{t-1}}e^{g_y}(1 + g_{n,t-1})1+gX,t​=X^t−1​X^t​​egy​(1+gn,t−1​)
    (83)

    where gn,t−1g_{n,t-1}gn,t−1​ is population growth from period t−1t-1t−1 to ttt. The options are:

    • 'Curr GDP': the growth of real GDP, X=YX = YX=Y

    • 'wage bill': the growth of total real labor earnings, X=wLX = wLX=wL (as in Latvia and Poland)

    • 'avg wage': the growth of real labor earnings per person, w^tL^tw^t−1L^t−1egy−1\frac{\hat{w}_t\hat{L}_t}{\hat{w}_{t-1}\hat{L}_{t-1}}e^{g_y} - 1w^t−1​L^t−1​w^t​L^t​​egy​−1 (as in Sweden and Norway)

    • 'r': the interest rate on household savings, rp,tr_{p,t}rp,t​

    • 'LR GDP' (the default): the constant long-run growth rate of real GDP, egy(1+gˉn)−1e^{g_y}(1 + \bar{g}_{n}) - 1egy​(1+gˉ​n​)−1

    All of these equal their long-run values in the steady state, except 'r', which equals the steady-state interest rate. Growth into period 0 uses the period-0 level as the level of the period before, and periods before the transition path take the period-0 rate. Some countries credit an average of past growth (for example, Italy credits the 5-year average of GDP growth); the parameter ndc_growth_avg_years sets the number of years averaged, with the rate credited in period ttt being the arithmetic mean of the rates in that period and the preceding periods in the window.

  • δR,s,t\delta_{R,s,t}δR,s,t​ is the conversion coefficient and its calculation is detailed below. It, like RRR and τp\tau^pτp, takes the values (k_ret, indR) that apply to the household’s birth cohort at the age and period in which the benefit is paid, so that a reform entered through pension_regimes with a max_age_at_start changes the formula only for the cohorts it covers.

δR=(dirR+indR−k)−1\delta_{R} = (dir_{R} + ind_{R} - k)^{-1}δR​=(dirR​+indR​−k)−1
(84)

where kkk is an adjustment that takes into account the number of payments per year. In particular, k=0.5−(6/13n)k=0.5 - (6/13n)k=0.5−(6/13n), where nnn is the number of payments per year. So if the payments are made monthly, n=12n=12n=12 and thus k=0.4615k=0.4615k=0.4615.

The dirR,tdir_{R, t}dirR,t​ term is an adjustment to make the payments actuarially fair given mortality risk. It is the expected discounted number of payments to a household that is alive at retirement age RRR and retires in period ttt:

dirR,t=∑k=0E+S−R[∏i=0k−1(1−ρ^R+i,t+i)](1+g^y,t)−kdir_{R, t} = \sum_{k=0}^{E+S-R}\left[\prod_{i=0}^{k-1}(1-\hat{\rho}_{R+i, t+i})\right](1+\hat{g}_{y, t})^{-k}dirR,t​=k=0∑E+S−R​[i=0∏k−1​(1−ρ^​R+i,t+i​)](1+g^​y,t​)−k
(85)

where the empty product (for k=0k=0k=0) equals one. The timing follows the household’s problem: ρs\rho_{s}ρs​ is the probability that a household of age sss dies before reaching age s+1s+1s+1, so the first payment, at age RRR, is certain and the payment at age R+kR+kR+k is received only if the household survives ages RRR through R+k−1R+k-1R+k−1. g^y,t\hat{g}_{y, t}g^​y,t​ is the rate used to discount payments, chosen with dir_growth_rate from the same options as ndc_growth_rate (without averaging). A household that retires in period ttt uses the value of that rate in period ttt for all of its payments, as countries typically fix a norm rate in the divisor when a pension is awarded.

ρ^s,t\hat{\rho}_{s,t}ρ^​s,t​ are the mortality rates used in the pension system, the model’s mortality rates averaged over lifetime income groups with the population weights λj\lambda_jλj​. The parameter ndc_mortality determines which rates apply. With 'cohort' (the default), ρ^R+i,t+i\hat{\rho}_{R+i, t+i}ρ^​R+i,t+i​ are the rates the retiring cohort faces at each age as it ages through the transition path, as written above. With 'period', the rates are those of the period of retirement, ρ^R+i,t\hat{\rho}_{R+i, t}ρ^​R+i,t​ (a period life table). With 'steady state', every cohort uses the steady-state rates ρ^R+i\hat{\rho}_{R+i}ρ^​R+i​. The three coincide in the steady state.

Finally, indRind_{R}indR​ is an adjustment for survivor benefits. Since we model households (and not individuals), we set indR=0ind_{R} = 0indR​=0 by default. This can be changed with the parameter indR if one would like to account for the fact that households lose members over time.

Given this pension system, the partial derivatives from the household section are given by:

∂θj,u,t+u−s∂nj,s,t={τtpwtej,s(1+gNDC,t)u−sδR,t,if s<R−10,if s≥R\frac{\partial \theta_{j,u,t+u-s}}{\partial n_{j,s,t}} = \begin{cases} \tau^{p}_{t}w_{t}e_{j,s}(1+g_{NDC,t})^{u - s}\delta_{R,t}, & \text{if}\ s<R-1 \\ 0, & \text{if}\ s \geq R \\ \end{cases}∂nj,s,t​∂θj,u,t+u−s​​={τtp​wt​ej,s​(1+gNDC,t​)u−sδR,t​,0,​if s<R−1if s≥R​
(86)
Points system¶

Under a points system, the pension amount is given as:

pensionj,s,t=∑s=ER−1wtej,s,tnj,s,t×vt∀s≥Rt−spension_{j,s,t} = \sum_{s=E}^{R-1}w_{t}e_{j,s,t}n_{j,s,t}\times v_{t} \quad \forall s \geq R_{t-s}pensionj,s,t​=s=E∑R−1​wt​ej,s,t​nj,s,t​×vt​∀s≥Rt−s​
(87)

where vtv_{t}vt​ is the value of a point at time ttt

Given this pension system, the partial derivatives from the household section are given by:

∂θj,u,t+u−s∂nj,s,t={0,if s<Rwtej,svt,if s≥R\frac{\partial \theta_{j,u,t+u-s}}{\partial n_{j,s,t}} = \begin{cases} 0 , & \text{if}\ s < R \\ w_{t}e_{j,s}v_{t}, & \text{if}\ s \geq R \\ \end{cases}∂nj,s,t​∂θj,u,t+u−s​​={0,wt​ej,s​vt​,​if s<Rif s≥R​
(88)
Hybrid defined benefit and notional defined contribution system¶

The hybrid system pays a defined benefit on labor income up to a cutoff and a notional defined contribution benefit on labor income in a band above that cutoff. The two cutoffs are set relative to average labor income in the first model period, f1,tyˉf_{1,t} \bar{y}f1,t​yˉ​ and f2,tyˉf_{2,t} \bar{y}f2,t​yˉ​ with 0≤f1,t≤f2,t0 \leq f_{1,t} \leq f_{2,t}0≤f1,t​≤f2,t​ in every period, where f1,tf_{1,t}f1,t​ is the parameter factor1_db_ndc_hybrid, f2,tf_{2,t}f2,t​ is the parameter factor2_db_ndc_hybrid, and yˉ\bar{y}yˉ​ is the parameter avg_labor_inc_t1_model_units. The value yˉ\bar{y}yˉ​ is the average labor income in the current (first) period in model units, taken from an outside model, so the cutoffs do not depend on endogenous variables such as the wage. The user must either supply their own series for each of factor1_db_ndc_hybrid and factor2_db_ndc_hybrid, or supply a single scalar in the list. A series is entered as a list of two or more values by year, starting in the base year, and every year after the last value entered keeps that value; the two lists need not have the same length. A single scalar is the initial factor f1,0f_{1,0}f1,0​ (or f2,0f_{2,0}f2,0​) of a path that has the growth trend removed from it, f1,t=f1,0/egytf_{1,t} = f_{1,0}/e^{g_y t}f1,t​=f1,0​/egy​t, which reflects a type of inflation indexation (equation (89) below). The defaults are the scalars f1,0=1.0f_{1,0} = 1.0f1,0​=1.0 and f2,0=2.0f_{2,0} = 2.0f2,0​=2.0, with yˉ=1.0\bar{y} = 1.0yˉ​=1.0, so by default the cutoffs are indexed in this way. To hold a factor constant instead, enter the same value twice, for example [1.0, 1.0]. The cutoffs that apply to any labor income are those of the period in which it was earned, so a change in the cutoffs affects the benefits of current workers only through the income they earn after the change, and leaves the benefits earned in earlier years unchanged.

How the cutoffs are indexed over time is set by the path of the factors. Because yˉ\bar{y}yˉ​ is in stationarized model units (labor income divided by egyte^{g_y t}egy​t), the cutoffs in levels are f1,tyˉegytf_{1,t}\bar{y}e^{g_y t}f1,t​yˉ​egy​t and f2,tyˉegytf_{2,t}\bar{y}e^{g_y t}f2,t​yˉ​egy​t:

  • Constant factors, f1,t=f1,0f_{1,t} = f_{1,0}f1,t​=f1,0​, give cutoffs that grow with labor augmenting technological change, at rate gyg_ygy​.

  • An indexed system, in which the cutoffs stay fixed in real terms at their initial level, sets the factors as below. This is the path the model builds when a factor is entered as a single scalar.

    f1,t=f1,0egytandf2,t=f2,0egyt f_{1,t} = \frac{f_{1,0}}{e^{g_y t}} \quad\text{and}\quad f_{2,t} = \frac{f_{2,0}}{e^{g_y t}}f1,t​=egy​tf1,0​​andf2,t​=egy​tf2,0​​
    (89)

    so that the cutoffs are f1,tyˉ=f1,0yˉe−gytf_{1,t}\bar{y} = f_{1,0}\bar{y}e^{-g_y t}f1,t​yˉ​=f1,0​yˉ​e−gy​t and f2,tyˉ=f2,0yˉe−gytf_{2,t}\bar{y} = f_{2,0}\bar{y}e^{-g_y t}f2,t​yˉ​=f2,0​yˉ​e−gy​t in model units, where f1,0f_{1,0}f1,0​ and f2,0f_{2,0}f2,0​ are the initial factor values and gyg_ygy​ is the growth rate of labor augmenting technological change per model period. With gy>0g_y > 0gy​>0 these factors fall toward zero, and the steady state uses the last value of each path, so in the long run nearly all labor income lies above both cutoffs and earns no benefit.

  • Any other kind of indexation is some other transformation of the path of f1,tf_{1,t}f1,t​ and f2,tf_{2,t}f2,t​. For example, cutoffs that grow at rate gcg_cgc​ per model period in real terms have f1,t=f1,0e(gc−gy)tf_{1,t} = f_{1,0}e^{(g_c - g_y)t}f1,t​=f1,0​e(gc​−gy​)t.

Labor income yj,s,t=wtej,s,tnj,s,ty_{j,s,t} = w_t e_{j,s,t} n_{j,s,t}yj,s,t​=wt​ej,s,t​nj,s,t​ is split into the following parts:

  • Labor income up to f1,tyˉf_{1,t} \bar{y}f1,t​yˉ​ earns a defined benefit, computed with the formula and parameters (RRR, nynyny, CyCyCy, αDB\alpha^{DB}αDB) of the defined benefit system applied to this capped income, min⁡{yj,s,t,f1,tyˉ}\min\{y_{j,s,t}, f_{1,t} \bar{y}\}min{yj,s,t​,f1,t​yˉ​}.

  • Labor income between f1,tyˉf_{1,t} \bar{y}f1,t​yˉ​ and f2,tyˉf_{2,t} \bar{y}f2,t​yˉ​ earns a notional defined contribution benefit, paid in addition to the defined benefit. The household’s notional account is credited with τpmax⁡{min⁡{yj,s,t,f2,tyˉ}−f1,tyˉ,0}\tau^{p} \max\{\min\{y_{j,s,t}, f_{2,t} \bar{y}\} - f_{1,t} \bar{y}, 0\}τpmax{min{yj,s,t​,f2,t​yˉ​}−f1,t​yˉ​,0}, and the benefit is computed with the formula and parameters (τp\tau^pτp, the credited rate gNDCg_{NDC}gNDC​ set by ndc_growth_rate and ndc_growth_avg_years, and the conversion coefficient δR\delta_RδR​ with its discount rate dir_growth_rate) of the notional defined contribution system.

  • Labor income above f2,tyˉf_{2,t} \bar{y}f2,t​yˉ​ earns no pension benefit.

The cutoffs determine only which income earns which benefit. They do not change what the household pays: as under the other pension systems, the payroll tax tau_payroll applies to all labor income yj,s,ty_{j,s,t}yj,s,t​, with no cap, and the notional rate tau_p is used only to credit the notional account, not deducted from household income.

Define the labor income in each band as

yj,s,tDB=min⁡{wtej,s,tnj,s,t,f1,tyˉ}andyj,s,tNDC=max⁡{min⁡{wtej,s,tnj,s,t,f2,tyˉ}−f1,tyˉ,0} y^{DB}_{j,s,t} = \min\{w_t e_{j,s,t}n_{j,s,t}, f_{1,t}\bar{y}\} \quad\text{and}\quad y^{NDC}_{j,s,t} = \max\bigl\{\min\{w_t e_{j,s,t}n_{j,s,t}, f_{2,t}\bar{y}\} - f_{1,t}\bar{y}, 0\bigr\}yj,s,tDB​=min{wt​ej,s,t​nj,s,t​,f1,t​yˉ​}andyj,s,tNDC​=max{min{wt​ej,s,t​nj,s,t​,f2,t​yˉ​}−f1,t​yˉ​,0}
(90)

The pension amount under the hybrid system is then the sum of the two benefits:

pensionj,s,t=[∑u=R−nyR−1yj,u,t−s+uDBny]×Cy×αj,s,tDB+[∑u=ER−1τu,t−s+upyj,u,t−s+uNDC∏a=u+1R−1(1+gNDC,t−s+a)]δR,s,t∀s≥R\begin{split} pension_{j,s,t} = &\biggl[\frac{\sum_{u=R-ny}^{R-1}y^{DB}_{j,u,t-s+u}}{ny}\biggr]\times Cy \times \alpha^{DB}_{j,s,t} \\ &+ \biggl[\sum_{u=E}^{R-1}\tau^{p}_{u,t-s+u}y^{NDC}_{j,u,t-s+u}\prod_{a=u+1}^{R-1}(1 + g_{NDC,t-s+a})\biggr]\delta_{R,s,t} \quad \forall s \geq R \end{split}pensionj,s,t​=​[ny∑u=R−nyR−1​yj,u,t−s+uDB​​]×Cy×αj,s,tDB​+[u=E∑R−1​τu,t−s+up​yj,u,t−s+uNDC​a=u+1∏R−1​(1+gNDC,t−s+a​)]δR,s,t​∀s≥R​
(91)

where, as in the separate systems, each sum runs over the household’s own earnings history (so yj,u,t−s+uDBy^{DB}_{j,u,t-s+u}yj,u,t−s+uDB​ and yj,u,t−s+uNDCy^{NDC}_{j,u,t-s+u}yj,u,t−s+uNDC​ use the cutoffs f1,t−s+uyˉf_{1,t-s+u}\bar{y}f1,t−s+u​yˉ​ and f2,t−s+uyˉf_{2,t-s+u}\bar{y}f2,t−s+u​yˉ​ of the period in which the household was age uuu) and the parameters are those that apply to the household’s birth cohort. Along the transition path the notional balances are credited with the same time-varying rates as under the notional defined contribution system. Setting f1,tf_{1,t}f1,t​ above all labor income gives the defined benefit system, and setting f1,t=0f_{1,t} = 0f1,t​=0 with f2,tf_{2,t}f2,t​ above all labor income gives the notional defined contribution system. As in the other systems, the benefit is scaled by replacement_rate_adjust.

Given this pension system, the partial derivative of the benefit with respect to labor supply at a working age s<Rs < Rs<R is the defined benefit derivative in equation (81) when the household’s labor income is below f1,tyˉf_{1,t} \bar{y}f1,t​yˉ​, the notional defined contribution derivative in equation (86) when it is between f1,tyˉf_{1,t} \bar{y}f1,t​yˉ​ and f2,tyˉf_{2,t} \bar{y}f2,t​yˉ​, and zero when it is above f2,tyˉf_{2,t} \bar{y}f2,t​yˉ​.

Aggregate Pension Spending¶

Total pension spending is the sum of the pension payments to each household in the model:

Pensionst=∑j=1J∑s=E+1E+Spensionj,s,tωs,tλj∀tPensions_{t} = \sum_{j=1}^{J}\sum_{s=E+1}^{E+S} pension_{j,s,t}\omega_{s,t}\lambda_j \quad\forall tPensionst​=j=1∑J​s=E+1∑E+S​pensionj,s,t​ωs,t​λj​∀t
(92)

Lump sum transfers:¶

Aggregate non-pension transfers to households are assumed to be a fixed fraction αtr\alpha_{tr}αtr​ of GDP each period:

TRt=gtr,t αtr Yt∀t TR_t = g_{tr,t}\:\alpha_{tr}\: Y_t \quad\forall tTRt​=gtr,t​αtr​Yt​∀t
(93)

The time dependent multiplier gtr,tg_{tr,t}gtr,t​ in front of the right-hand-side of (93) will equal 1 in most initial periods. It will potentially deviate from 1 in some future periods in order to provide a closure rule that ensures a stable long-run debt-to-GDP ratio. We will discuss the closure rule in Section Budget Closure Rule.

Universal basic income¶

[TODO: This section is far along but needs to be updated.]

Universal basic income (UBI) transfers show up in the household budget constraint (26). Household amounts of UBI can vary by household age sss, lifetime income group jjj, and time period ttt. These transfers are represented by ubij,s,tubi_{j,s,t}ubij,s,t​.

Calculating UBI¶

Household transfers in model units of the numeraire good ubij,s,tubi_{j,s,t}ubij,s,t​ are a function of five policy parameters described in the default_parameters.json file (ubi_growthadj, ubi_nom_017, ubi_nom_1864, ubi_nom_65p, and ubi_nom_max). Three additional parameters provide information on household structure by age, lifetime income group, and year: [ubi_num_017_mat, ubi_num_1864_mat, ubi_num_65p_mat].

As a convenience to users, UBI policy parameters ubi_nom_017, ubi_nom_1864, ubi_nom_65p, and ubi_nom_max are entered as nominal amounts (e.g., in dollars or pounds). The parameter ubi_nom_017 represents the nominal value of the UBI transfer to each household per dependent child age 17 and under. The parameter ubi_nom_1864 represents the nominal value of the UBI transfer to each household per adult between the ages of 18 and 64. And ubi_nom_65p is the nominal value of UBI transfer to each household per senior 65 and over. The maximum UBI benefit per household, ubi_nom_max, is also a nominal amount. From these parameters, the model computes nominal UBI payments to each household in the model:

ubij,s,t=0nom=min⁡(ubi_nom_max,ubi_nom_017∗ubi_num_017_matj,s+ubi_nom_1864∗ubi_num_1864_matj,s+ubi_nom_65p∗ubi_num_65p_matj,s)∀j,s \begin{split} ubi^{nom}_{j,s,t=0} = \min\Bigl(&\texttt{ubi\_nom\_max}, \\ &\texttt{ubi\_nom\_017} * \texttt{ubi\_num\_017\_mat}_{j,s} + \\ &\texttt{ubi\_nom\_1864} * \texttt{ubi\_num\_1864\_mat}_{j,s} + \\ &\texttt{ubi\_nom\_65p} * \texttt{ubi\_num\_65p\_mat}_{j,s}\Bigr) \quad\forall j,s \end{split}ubij,s,t=0nom​=min(​ubi_nom_max,ubi_nom_017∗ubi_num_017_matj,s​+ubi_nom_1864∗ubi_num_1864_matj,s​+ubi_nom_65p∗ubi_num_65p_matj,s​)∀j,s​
(94)

The rest of the time periods of the household UBI transfer and the respective steady-states are determined by whether the UBI is growth adjusted or not as given in the ubi_growthadj boolean parameter. The following two sections cover these two cases.

UBI specification not adjusted for economic growth¶

A non-growth adjusted UBI (ubi_growthadj = False) is one in which the initial nonstationary nominal-valued t=0t=0t=0 UBI matrix ubij,s,t=0nomubi^{nom}_{j,s,t=0}ubij,s,t=0nom​ does not grow, while the economy’s long-run growth rate is gyg_ygy​ for the most common parameterization is positive (gy>0g_y>0gy​>0).

ubij,s,tnom=ubij,s,t=0nom∀j,s,t ubi^{nom}_{j,s,t} = ubi^{nom}_{j,s,t=0} \quad\forall j,s,tubij,s,tnom​=ubij,s,t=0nom​∀j,s,t
(95)

As described in chapter Stationarization, the stationarized UBI transfer to each household ubi^j,s,t\hat{ubi}_{j,s,t}ubi^j,s,t​ is the nonstationary transfer divided by the growth rate since the initial period. When the long-run economic growth rate is positive gy>0g_y>0gy​>0 and the UBI specification is not growth-adjusted, the steady-state stationary UBI household transfer is zero ubi‾j,s=0\overline{ubi}_{j,s}=0ubij,s​=0 for all lifetime income groups jjj and ages sss as time periods ttt go to infinity. However, to simplify, we assume in this case that the stationarized steady-state UBI transfer matrix to households is the stationarized value of that matrix in period TTT.[4]

ubi‾j,s=ubij,s,t=T∀j,s \overline{ubi}_{j,s} = ubi_{j,s,t=T} \quad\forall j,subij,s​=ubij,s,t=T​∀j,s
(96)

Note that in non-growth-adjusted case, if gy<0g_y<0gy​<0, then the stationary value of ubi^j,s,t\hat{ubi}_{j,s,t}ubi^j,s,t​ is going to infinity as ttt goes to infinity. Therefore, a UBI specification must be growth adjusted for any assumed negative long run growth gy<0g_y<0gy​<0.[5]

Spending in the reform simulation¶

While aggregate spending on GGG, TRTRTR, and IgI_gIg​ in the baseline simulation are set as fractions of GDP, in the reform simulation, these spending amounts can be set in two different ways. The method is controlled by the baseline_spending parameter. If baseline_spending=False, the behavior of these spending is analgous to that in the baseline simulation; they are set as fractions of GDP, in this case GDP in the reform simulation. Thus, with the default assumption of baseline_spending it’s assumed that spending levels in these three categories are function of GDP in the reform. In this case, users will see that, even with the parameters αG\alpha_GαG​, αT\alpha_TαT​, and αI\alpha_IαI​ are unchanged, the level of spending will change in the reform if GDP in the reform is different.

With the assumption of baseline_spending=True, the level of spending in the reform is held to the level of spending in the baseline. If the user wishes to adjust the level of spending, relative to the baseline level, in the reform, then the parameters alpha_bs_G, alpha_bs_T, and alpha_bs_I can be used to proportionally increase or decrease the levels of spending on GGG, TRTRTR, and IgI_gIg​ in the reform simulation, relative to the levels in the baseline simulation. Note that the alpha_bs_* parameters are time varying, so the proportional change in spending can be different across time. E.g., for government consumption expenditures, we’d have the reform amount of GGG determined as:

Gtreform=αG,tBSGtbaseline G^{reform}_t = \alpha^{BS}_{G,t}G^{baseline}_{t}Gtreform​=αG,tBS​Gtbaseline​
(97)

Foreign aid to the domestic government, FAtFA_tFAt​, is treated the same way. In the baseline simulation, and in the reform when baseline_spending=False, foreign aid is a fraction αFA,t\alpha_{FA,t}αFA,t​ of GDP. When baseline_spending=True, foreign aid in the reform is held to its level in the baseline, scaled by the time-varying parameter alpha_bs_FA:

FAtreform=αFA,tBSFAtbaseline FA^{reform}_t = \alpha^{BS}_{FA,t}FA^{baseline}_{t}FAtreform​=αFA,tBS​FAtbaseline​
(98)

This means that changes to alpha_FA in the reform have no effect when baseline_spending=True; use alpha_bs_FA to change the level of foreign aid relative to the baseline instead.

Note that the budget closure rule (described in Section ref{SecUnbalGBCcloseRule}) still takes effect in the case of baseline_spending=True. What this means is that the relation described above holds until the period in which the closure rules takes effect. Once the closure rule begins, the path of GGG (and/or TRTRTR, depending on the closure rule used) will adjust as determined by the rule to close the government budget in the long run.

(100)

We define total government revenue from taxes in terms of the numeraire good as the following,

Revt=∑m=1M[τm,tcorp(pm,tYm,t−wtLm,t)−(τm,tcorpδm,tτ+τm,tinvδM,t)Km,t]⏟corporate income tax revenue+∑s=E+1E+S∑j=1Jλjωs,tτs,tetr,xy(xj,s,t,yj,s,t)(xj,s,t+yj,s,t)⏟household income tax revenue+∑s=E+1E+S∑j=1J∑i=1Iλjωs,tτi,tcpi,tci,j,s,t⏟consumption tax revenue+∑s=E+1E+S∑j=1Jλjωs,tτtetr,wbj,s,t⏟wealth tax revenue+∑s=E+1E+S∑j=1Jλjωs,tτtbqbqj,s,t⏟bequest tax revenue∀t\begin{aligned} Rev_t &= \underbrace{\sum_{m=1}^M\Bigl[\tau^{corp}_{m,t}\bigl(p_{m,t}Y_{m,t} - w_t L_{m,t}\bigr) - \bigl(\tau^{corp}_{m,t}\delta^\tau_{m,t} + \tau^{inv}_{m,t}\delta_{M,t}\bigr)K_{m,t}\Bigr]}_{\text{corporate income tax revenue}} \\ &\quad + \underbrace{\sum_{s=E+1}^{E+S}\sum_{j=1}^J\lambda_j\omega_{s,t}\tau^{etr,xy}_{s,t}\left(x_{j,s,t},y_{j,s,t}\right)\bigl(x_{j,s,t} + y_{j,s,t}\bigr)}_{\text{household income tax revenue}} \\ &\quad + \underbrace{\sum_{s=E+1}^{E+S}\sum_{j=1}^J\sum_{i=1}^I\lambda_j\omega_{s,t}\tau^{c}_{i,t}p_{i,t}c_{i,j,s,t}}_{\text{consumption tax revenue}} \\ &\quad + \underbrace{\sum_{s=E+1}^{E+S}\sum_{j=1}^J\lambda_j\omega_{s,t}\tau^{etr,w}_{t}b_{j,s,t}}_{\text{wealth tax revenue}}\\ &\quad + \underbrace{\sum_{s=E+1}^{E+S}\sum_{j=1}^J\lambda_j\omega_{s,t}\tau^{bq}_{t}bq_{j,s,t}}_{\text{bequest tax revenue}} \quad\forall t \end{aligned}Revt​​=corporate income tax revenuem=1∑M​[τm,tcorp​(pm,t​Ym,t​−wt​Lm,t​)−(τm,tcorp​δm,tτ​+τm,tinv​δM,t​)Km,t​]​​+household income tax revenues=E+1∑E+S​j=1∑J​λj​ωs,t​τs,tetr,xy​(xj,s,t​,yj,s,t​)(xj,s,t​+yj,s,t​)​​+consumption tax revenues=E+1∑E+S​j=1∑J​i=1∑I​λj​ωs,t​τi,tc​pi,t​ci,j,s,t​​​+wealth tax revenues=E+1∑E+S​j=1∑J​λj​ωs,t​τtetr,w​bj,s,t​​​+bequest tax revenues=E+1∑E+S​j=1∑J​λj​ωs,t​τtbq​bqj,s,t​​​∀t​
(101)

where household labor income is defined as xj,s,t≡wtej,snj,s,tx_{j,s,t}\equiv w_t e_{j,s}n_{j,s,t}xj,s,t​≡wt​ej,s​nj,s,t​ and capital income yj,s,t≡rp,tbj,s,ty_{j,s,t}\equiv r_{p,t} b_{j,s,t}yj,s,t​≡rp,t​bj,s,t​.

Government Budget Constraint¶

Let the level of government debt in period ttt be given by DtD_tDt​. The government budget constraint requires that government revenue RevtRev_tRevt​, external foreign assistance, FAtFA_tFAt​, plus the budget deficit (Dt+1−DtD_{t+1} - D_tDt+1​−Dt​) equal expenditures on interest on the debt, government spending on public goods GtG_tGt​, total infrastructure investments Ig,tI_{g,t}Ig,t​, total pension outlays, total transfer payments to households TRtTR_tTRt​, and UBItUBI_tUBIt​ every period ttt,

Dt+1+Revt+FAt=(1+rgov,t)Dt+Gt+Ig,t+Pensionst+TRt+UBIt∀t D_{t+1} + Rev_t + FA_t = (1 + r_{gov,t})D_t + G_t + I_{g,t} + Pensions_t + TR_t + UBI_t \quad\forall tDt+1​+Revt​+FAt​=(1+rgov,t​)Dt​+Gt​+Ig,t​+Pensionst​+TRt​+UBIt​∀t
(102)

where rgov,tr_{gov,t}rgov,t​ is the interest rate paid by the government defined in equation (108) below, GtG_{t}Gt​ is government spending on public goods, Ig,tI_{g,t}Ig,t​ is total government spending on infrastructure investment, TRtTR_{t}TRt​ are non-pension government transfers, and UBItUBI_tUBIt​ is the total UBI transfer outlays across households in time ttt. All variables in (102) are real variables denominated in units of current-period output in industry MMM the numeraire (pM,t=1p_{M,t}=1pM,t​=1 for all ttt).

We assume that government spending on public goods in terms of the numeraire good is a fixed fraction of GDP each period in the initial periods.

Gt=gg,t αg Yt∀t G_t = g_{g,t}\:\alpha_{g}\: Y_t \quad\forall tGt​=gg,t​αg​Yt​∀t
(103)

Similar to transfers TRtTR_tTRt​, the time dependent multiplier gg,tg_{g,t}gg,t​ in front of the right-hand-side of (103) will equal 1 in most initial periods. It will potentially deviate from 1 in some future periods in order to provide a closure rule that ensures a stable long-run debt-to-GDP ratio. We make this more specific in the next section.

Total government infrastructure investment spending, Ig,tI_{g,t}Ig,t​ is assumed to be a time-dependent fraction of GDP.

Ig,t=αI,t Yt∀t I_{g,t} = \alpha_{I,t}\: Y_t \quad\forall tIg,t​=αI,t​Yt​∀t
(104)

The government also chooses what percent of total infrastructure investment goes to each industry αI,m,t\alpha_{I,m,t}αI,m,t​, although these are exogenously calibrated parameters in the model.

Ig,m,t=αI,m,t Ig,t∀m,t I_{g,m,t} = \alpha_{I,m,t}\: I_{g,t} \quad\forall m,tIg,m,t​=αI,m,t​Ig,t​∀m,t
(105)

The stock of public capital (i.e., infrastructure) in each industry mmm evolves according to the law of motion,

Kg,m,t+1=(1−δg)Kg,m,t+(1−ϕg)Ig,m,t∀m,t K_{g,m,t+1} = (1 - \delta_g) K_{g,m,t} + (1 - \phi_g) I_{g,m,t} \quad\forall m,tKg,m,t+1​=(1−δg​)Kg,m,t​+(1−ϕg​)Ig,m,t​∀m,t
(106)

where δg\delta_gδg​ is the depreciation rate on infrastructure and ϕg\phi_gϕg​ (infra_investment_leakage_rate) is the fraction of infrastructure investment lost to leakage (e.g., corruption or other frictions). The stock of public capital in each industry mmm complements labor and private capital in the production function of the representative firm, in Equation (46).

Aggregate spending on UBI at time ttt is the sum of UBI payments across all households at time ttt:

UBIt≡∑s=E+1E+S∑j=1Jλjωs,tubij,s,t∀t UBI_t \equiv \sum_{s=E+1}^{E+S}\sum_{j=1}^J \lambda_j\omega_{s,t} ubi_{j,s,t} \quad\forall tUBIt​≡s=E+1∑E+S​j=1∑J​λj​ωs,t​ubij,s,t​∀t
(107)

Interest Rate on Government Debt and Household Savings¶

Despite the model having no aggregate risk, it may be helpful to build in an interest rate differential between the rate of return on private capital and the interest rate on government debt. Doing so helps to add realism by including a risk premium. OG-Core allows users to set an exogenous wedge between these two rates. OG-Core also allows for the risk premium on debt to be a quadratic function of the debt-to-GDP ratio. The interest rate on government debt is given by:

rgov,t=(1−τd,t)rt−μd+β1DtYt+β2(DtYt)2 r_{gov, t} = (1 - \tau_{d, t})r_{t} - \mu_{d} + \beta_{1}\frac{D_t}{Y_t} + \beta_{2}\left(\frac{D_t}{Y_t}\right)^2rgov,t​=(1−τd,t​)rt​−μd​+β1​Yt​Dt​​+β2​(Yt​Dt​​)2
(108)

where rtr_trt​ is the marginal product of capital faced by firms. The two parameters, τd,t\tau_{d,t}τd,t​ and μd,t\mu_{d,t}μd,t​ can be used to allow for a government interest rate that is a percentage hair cut from the market rate or a government interest rate with a constant risk premium. The parameters β1\beta_1β1​ and β2\beta_2β2​ can be used to allow for a quadratic risk premium on government debt that is a function of the debt-to-GDP ratio.

Budget Closure Rule¶

If total government transfers to households TRtTR_tTRt​ and government spending on public goods GtG_tGt​ are both fixed fractions of GDP, one can imagine corporate and household tax structures that cause the debt level of the government to either tend toward infinity or to negative infinity, depending on whether too little revenue or too much revenue is raised, respectively.

A virtue of dynamic general equilibrium models is that the model must be stationary in the long-run in order to solve it. That is, no variables can be indefinitely growing as time moves forward. The labor augmenting productivity growth gyg_ygy​ from Chapter Firms and the potential population growth g~n,t\tilde{g}_{n,t}g~​n,t​ from the calibration chapter on demographics in the country-specific repository documentation render the model nonstationary. But we show how to stationarize the model against those two sources of growth in Chapter Stationarization. However, even after stationarizing the effects of productivity and population growth, the model could be rendered nonstationary and, therefore, not solvable if government debt were becoming too positive or too negative too quickly.

For the model to be stationary, the debt-to-GDP ratio must be stable in the long run. Because the debt-to-GDP ratio is a quotient of two macroeconomic variables, the non-stationary and stationary versions of this ratio are equivalent. Let TTT be some time period in the future. The stationarizing assumption is the following,

Dt=αDYt⇒DtYt=αDfort≥T D_t = \alpha_D Y_t \quad\Rightarrow\quad \frac{D_t}{Y_t} = \alpha_D \quad\text{for}\quad t\geq TDt​=αD​Yt​⇒Yt​Dt​​=αD​fort≥T
(109)

where αD\alpha_DαD​ is a scalar long-run value of the debt-to-GDP ratio. This long-run stability condition on the debt-to-GDP ratio clearly applies to the steady-state as well as any point in the time path for t>Tt>Tt>T.

We detail three possible closure-rule options here for stabilizing the debt-to-GDP ratio in the long run, although OG-Core only has the capability currently to execute the first closure rule that adjusts government spending GtG_tGt​. We expect to have the other two rules implemented as OG-Core options soon. Each rule uses some combination of changes in government spending on public goods GtG_tGt​ and government transfers to households TRtTR_tTRt​ to stabilize the debt-to-GDP ratio in the long-run.

  1. Change only government spending on public goods GtG_tGt​.

  2. Change only government transfers to households TRtTR_tTRt​.

  3. Change both government spending GtG_tGt​ and transfers TRtTR_tTRt​ by the same percentage.

Change government spending only¶

We specify a closure rule that is automatically implemented after some period TG1T_{G1}TG1​ to stabilize government debt as a percent of GDP (debt-to-GDP ratio) by period TG2T_{G2}TG2​. Let αD\alpha_DαD​ represent the long-run debt-to-GDP ratio at which we want the economy to eventually settle.

Gt=gg,t αg Ytwheregg,t={1 ift<TG1[ρdαDYt+(1−ρd)Dt]−(1+rgov,t)Dt−Ig,t−TRt−UBIt+Revt+FAtαgYtifTG1≤t<TG2αDYt−(1+rgov,t)Dt−Ig,t−TRt−UBIt+Revt+FAtαgYt   ift≥TG2andgtr,t=1∀t\begin{split} &G_t = g_{g,t}\:\alpha_{g}\: Y_t \\ &\text{where}\quad g_{g,t} = \begin{cases} 1 \qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\quad\:\text{if}\quad t < T_{G1} \\ \frac{\left[\rho_{d}\alpha_{D}Y_{t} + (1-\rho_{d})D_{t}\right] - (1+r_{gov,t})D_{t} - I_{g,t} - TR_{t} - UBI_{t} + Rev_{t} + FA_{t}}{\alpha_g Y_t} \quad\text{if}\quad T_{G1}\leq t<T_{G2} \\ \frac{\alpha_{D}Y_{t} - (1+r_{gov,t})D_{t} - I_{g,t} - TR_{t} - UBI_{t} + Rev_{t} + FA_{t}}{\alpha_g Y_t} \qquad\qquad\quad\:\:\,\text{if}\quad t \geq T_{G2} \end{cases} \\ &\text{and}\quad g_{tr,t} = 1 \quad\forall t \end{split}​Gt​=gg,t​αg​Yt​wheregg,t​=⎩⎨⎧​1ift<TG1​αg​Yt​[ρd​αD​Yt​+(1−ρd​)Dt​]−(1+rgov,t​)Dt​−Ig,t​−TRt​−UBIt​+Revt​+FAt​​ifTG1​≤t<TG2​αg​Yt​αD​Yt​−(1+rgov,t​)Dt​−Ig,t​−TRt​−UBIt​+Revt​+FAt​​ift≥TG2​​andgtr,t​=1∀t​
(110)

The first case in (110) says that government spending GtG_tGt​ will be a fixed fraction αg\alpha_gαg​ of GDP YtY_tYt​ for every period before TG1T_{G1}TG1​. The second case specifies that, starting in period TG1T_{G1}TG1​ and continuing until before period TG2T_{G2}TG2​, government spending be adjusted to set tomorrow’s debt Dt+1D_{t+1}Dt+1​ to be a convex combination between its long-run stable level αDYt\alpha_D Y_tαD​Yt​ and the current debt level DtD_tDt​, where αD\alpha_DαD​ is a target debt-to-GDP ratio and ρd∈(0,1]\rho_d\in(0,1]ρd​∈(0,1] is the percent of the way to jump toward the target αDYt\alpha_D Y_tαD​Yt​ from the current debt level DtD_tDt​. The last case specifies that, for every period after TG2T_{G2}TG2​, government spending GtG_tGt​ is set such that the next-period debt be a fixed target percentage αD\alpha_DαD​ of GDP.

Change government transfers only¶

If government transfers to households are specified by (93) and the long-run debt-to-GDP ratio can only be stabilized by changing transfers, then the budget closure rule must be the following.

TRt=gtr,t αtr Ytwheregtr,t={1    ift<TG1[ρdαDYt+(1−ρd)Dt]−(1+rgov,t)Dt−Gt−Ig,t−UBIt+Revt+FAtαtrYtifTG1≤t<TG2αDYt−(1+rgov,t)Dt−Gt−Ig,t−UBIt+Revt+FAtαtrYt   ift≥TG2andgg,t=1∀t\begin{split} &TR_t = g_{tr,t}\:\alpha_{tr}\: Y_t \\ &\text{where}\quad g_{tr,t} = \begin{cases} 1 \qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\:\:\:\,\text{if}\quad t < T_{G1} \\ \frac{\left[\rho_{d}\alpha_{D}Y_{t} + (1-\rho_{d})D_{t}\right] - (1+r_{gov,t})D_{t} - G_{t} - I_{g,t} - UBI_{t} + Rev_{t} + FA_{t}}{\alpha_{tr} Y_t} \quad\text{if}\quad T_{G1}\leq t<T_{G2} \\ \frac{\alpha_{D}Y_{t} - (1+r_{gov,t})D_{t} - G_{t} - I_{g,t} - UBI_{t} + Rev_{t} + FA_{t}}{\alpha_{tr}Y_t} \qquad\qquad\quad\:\:\:\text{if}\quad t \geq T_{G2} \end{cases} \\ &\text{and}\quad g_{g,t} = 1 \quad\forall t \end{split}​TRt​=gtr,t​αtr​Yt​wheregtr,t​=⎩⎨⎧​1ift<TG1​αtr​Yt​[ρd​αD​Yt​+(1−ρd​)Dt​]−(1+rgov,t​)Dt​−Gt​−Ig,t​−UBIt​+Revt​+FAt​​ifTG1​≤t<TG2​αtr​Yt​αD​Yt​−(1+rgov,t​)Dt​−Gt​−Ig,t​−UBIt​+Revt​+FAt​​ift≥TG2​​andgg,t​=1∀t​
(111)

The first case in (111) says that government transfers TRtTR_tTRt​ will be a fixed fraction αtr\alpha_{tr}αtr​ of GDP YtY_tYt​ for every period before TG1T_{G1}TG1​. The second case specifies that, starting in period TG1T_{G1}TG1​ and continuing until before period TG2T_{G2}TG2​, government transfers be adjusted to set tomorrow’s debt Dt+1D_{t+1}Dt+1​ to be a convex combination between the target debt αDYt\alpha_D Y_tαD​Yt​ and the current debt level DtD_tDt​. The last case specifies that, for every period after TG2T_{G2}TG2​, government transfers TRtTR_tTRt​ are set such that the next-period debt be a fixed target percentage αD\alpha_DαD​ of GDP.

Change both government spending and transfers¶

In some cases, changing only government spending GtG_tGt​ or only government transfers TRtTR_tTRt​ will not be enough. That is, there exist policies for which a decrease in government spending to zero after period TG1T_{G1}TG1​ will not stabilize the debt-to-GDP ratio. And negative government spending on public goods does not make sense. [6] On the other hand, negative transfers do make sense. Notwithstanding, one might want the added stabilization ability of changing both government spending GtG_tGt​ and transfers TRtTR_tTRt​ to stabilize the long-run debt-to-GDP ratio.

In our specific form of this joint option, we assume that the factor by which we scale government spending and transfers is the same gg,t=gtr,tg_{g,t} = g_{tr,t}gg,t​=gtr,t​ for all ttt. We label this single scaling factor gtrg,tg_{trg,t}gtrg,t​.

gtrg,t≡gg,t=gtr,t∀t g_{trg,t}\equiv g_{g,t} = g_{tr,t} \quad\forall tgtrg,t​≡gg,t​=gtr,t​∀t
(112)

If government spending on public goods is specified by (103) and government transfers to households are specified by (93) and the long-run debt-to-GDP ratio can only be stabilized by changing both spending and transfers, then the budget closure rule must be the following.

Gt+TRt=gtrg,t(αg+αtr)Yt⇒Gt=gtrg,t αg YtandTRt=gtrg,t αtr Ytwheregtrg,t={1  ift<TG1[ρdαDYt+(1−ρd)Dt]−(1+rgov,t)Dt−Ig,t−UBIt+Revt+FAt(αg+αtr)YtifTG1≤t<TG2αDYt−(1+rgov,t)Dt−Ig,t−UBIt+Revt+FAt(αg+αtr)Yt   ift≥TG2\begin{split} &G_t + TR_t = g_{trg,t}\left(\alpha_g + \alpha_{tr}\right)Y_t \quad\Rightarrow\quad G_t = g_{trg,t}\:\alpha_g\: Y_t \quad\text{and}\quad TR_t = g_{trg,t}\:\alpha_{tr}\: Y_t \\ &\text{where}\quad g_{trg,t} = \begin{cases} 1 \qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\quad\:\,\text{if}\quad t < T_{G1} \\ \frac{\left[\rho_{d}\alpha_{D}Y_{t} + (1-\rho_{d})D_{t}\right] - (1+r_{gov,t})D_{t} - I_{g,t} - UBI_{t} + Rev_{t} + FA_{t}}{\left(\alpha_g + \alpha_{tr}\right)Y_t} \quad\text{if}\quad T_{G1}\leq t<T_{G2} \\ \frac{\alpha_{D}Y_{t} - (1+r_{gov,t})D_{t} - I_{g,t} - UBI_{t} + Rev_{t} + FA_{t}}{\left(\alpha_g + \alpha_{tr}\right)Y_t} \qquad\qquad\quad\:\:\:\text{if}\quad t \geq T_{G2} \end{cases} \end{split}​Gt​+TRt​=gtrg,t​(αg​+αtr​)Yt​⇒Gt​=gtrg,t​αg​Yt​andTRt​=gtrg,t​αtr​Yt​wheregtrg,t​=⎩⎨⎧​1ift<TG1​(αg​+αtr​)Yt​[ρd​αD​Yt​+(1−ρd​)Dt​]−(1+rgov,t​)Dt​−Ig,t​−UBIt​+Revt​+FAt​​ifTG1​≤t<TG2​(αg​+αtr​)Yt​αD​Yt​−(1+rgov,t​)Dt​−Ig,t​−UBIt​+Revt​+FAt​​ift≥TG2​​​
(113)

The first case in (113) says that government spending and government transfers TRtTR_tTRt​ will their respective fixed fractions αg\alpha_gαg​ and αtr\alpha_{tr}αtr​ of GDP YtY_tYt​ for every period before TG1T_{G1}TG1​. The second case specifies that, starting in period TG1T_{G1}TG1​ and continuing until before period TG2T_{G2}TG2​, government spending and transfers be adjusted by the same rate to set tomorrow’s debt Dt+1D_{t+1}Dt+1​ to be a convex combination between target debt αDYt\alpha_D Y_tαD​Yt​ and the current debt level DtD_tDt​. The last case specifies that, for every period after TG2T_{G2}TG2​, government spending and transfers are set such that the next-period debt be a fixed target percentage αD\alpha_DαD​ of GDP.

Each of these budget closure rules (110), (111), and (113) allows the government to run increasing deficits or surpluses in the short run (before period TG1T_{G1}TG1​). But then the adjustment rule is implemented gradually beginning in period t=TG1t=T_{G1}t=TG1​ to return the debt-to-GDP ratio back to its long-run target of αD\alpha_DαD​. Then the rule is implemented exactly in period TG2T_{G2}TG2​ by adjusting some combination of government spending GtG_tGt​ and transfers TRtTR_tTRt​ to set the debt Dt+1D_{t+1}Dt+1​ such that it is exactly αD\alpha_DαD​ proportion of GDP YtY_tYt​.

Some Caveats and Alternatives¶

OG-Core adjusts some combination of government spending GtG_tGt​ and government transfers TRtTR_tTRt​ as its closure rule instrument because of its simplicity and lack of distortionary effects. Since government spending does not enter into the household’s utility function, its level does not affect the solution of the household problem. In contrast, government transfers do appear in the household budget constraint. However, household decisions do not individually affect the amount of transfers, thereby rendering government transfers as exogenous from the household’s perspective. As an alternative, one could choose to adjust taxes to close the budget (or a combination of all of the government fiscal policy levers).

There is no guarantee that any of our stated closure rules (110), (111), or (113) is sufficient to stabilize the debt-to-GDP ratio in the long run. For large and growing deficits, the convex combination parameter ρd\rho_dρd​ might be too gradual, or the budget closure initial period TG1T_{G1}TG1​ might be too far in the future, or the target debt-to-GDP ratio αD\alpha_DαD​ might be too high. The existence of any of these problems might be manifest in the steady state computation stage. However, it is possible for the steady-state to exist, but for the time path to never reach it. These problems can be avoided by choosing conservative values for TG1T_{G1}TG1​, ρd\rho_dρd​, and αD\alpha_DαD​ that close the budget quickly.

And finally, in closure rules (110) and (113) in which government spending is used to stabilize the long-run budget, it is also possible that government spending is forced to be less than zero to make this happen. This would be the case if tax revenues bring in less than is needed to financed transfers and interest payments on the national debt. None of the equations we’ve specified above preclude that result, but it does raise conceptual difficulties. Namely, what does it mean for government spending to be negative? Is the government selling off public assets? We caution those using this budget closure rule to consider carefully how the budget is closed in the long run given their parameterization. We also note that such difficulties present themselves across all budget closure rules when analyzing tax or spending proposals that induce structural budget deficits. In particular, one probably needs a different closure instrument if government spending must be negative in the steady-state to hit your long-term debt-to-GDP target.
